title: Pseudodeterministic construction of primes at every length
formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a constant \(c\), and a sequence of primes \((p_{n})_{n\geq2}\), with \(2^{n-1}\leq p_{n}<2^{n}\), such that \(A\) runs in time \(O(n^{c})\) on input \(1^{n}\) and \[\Pr[A(1^{n})=p_{n}]\geq 2/3\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq2?\]

source_formulation.text: In the context of polynomial time pseudo-determinism, there are many fundamental problems with polynomial time randomized algorithms where the existence of pseudodeterministic polynomial time algorithms […]
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 12

context:
Primes can be generated in randomized polynomial time with high probability by sampling candidates and using polynomial-time primality testing. The resulting distribution typically spreads its mass over many primes. Pseudodeterminism asks for a reproducible output even though randomness is used internally.

The 2023 result of Chen, Lu, Oliveira, Ren and Santhanam, with a 2025 revised manuscript and 2026 journal publication, constructs a canonical prime in polynomial time on infinitely many input lengths. Its guarantee does not cover every sufficiently large length.

Theorem 1.1 gives an algorithm for each dense polynomial-time decidable property that almost always outputs either its canonical valid string or a failure symbol. The probability of actually producing the canonical string is at least \(1-2^{-n}\) only on infinitely many lengths. Allowing near-certain failure on other lengths is precisely weaker than the target here.

The same 2017 paragraph also asks about constructing irreducible degree-\(d\) polynomials over \(\mathbb F_{p}\) from a prime \(p\) and unary \(d\), and finding primitive roots modulo a prime when the factorization of \(p-1\) is supplied. These are retained as source context, not additional requirements or claimed equivalents of prime construction.
why: A canonical prime construction tests how far efficient randomized search can be made reproducible without fully removing randomness. It is a prominent concrete problem connecting derandomization, explicit constructions and computational number theory; extending the infinitely-often theorem would close its remaining length-coverage gap.
status_note: Read the original conclusion and definition of pseudodeterminism, and the December 2025 full revised prime-construction theorem. Checked publisher-deposited metadata for the April 2026 journal publication and searched through 12 September 2026. No unconditional uniform polynomial-time guarantee at every length was found. sentences: Given a length in unary, generate a prime with exactly that many binary digits in polynomial time.
For each length, independent runs must return the same fixed prime with probability at least two thirds.
The fixed prime may depend on the algorithm; it is not prescribed in advance.
The requirement must hold at every length of at least two bits.
The known polynomial-time construction meets this requirement only on infinitely many lengths.

references.title: Bipartite Perfect Matching in Pseudo-Deterministic NC

definitions:
The input \(1^{n}\) is unary: a string of \(n\) copies of the symbol 1. The output is the ordinary binary representation of an integer. An \(n\)-bit prime is an integer \(p\) in \([2^{n-1},2^{n})\) whose only positive divisors are 1 and \(p\). The domain begins at \(n=2\), since there is no one-bit prime.

The machine is a single classical probabilistic Turing machine, with independent unbiased random bits and a polynomial worst-case running-time bound on every random tape. There is no advice depending on \(n\), precomputed table of primes, oracle, or free preprocessing. All computation, including any primality tests, counts toward its time bound.

Pseudodeterminism means that for each fixed length there is one fixed prime \(p_{n}\) returned with the stated probability across independent executions. The prime may depend on the algorithm and on \(n\), but not on the execution’s random bits. It need not be the smallest \(n\)-bit prime or a prime prescribed in advance. The remaining probability mass may produce a failure symbol, another prime, or an invalid output.

The guarantee is required at every length. Success on infinitely many unbounded lengths alone does not suffice. A guarantee for all sufficiently large lengths would suffice, since finitely many shorter lengths can be handled by a fixed finite part of the algorithm.

The constant success probability is the usual bounded-error convention for pseudodeterminism. Independent repetitions followed by a majority output can amplify concentration on the same canonical prime with polynomial overhead. Merely finding some prime with high probability, while different runs usually return different primes, does not meet the requirement.

The source lists several distinct search tasks. This card explicitly selects prime generation as its main target; it does not assert that solving it is equivalent to making every randomized search problem pseudodeterministic.
answer_criterion: Construct such an algorithm and prove the polynomial bound and concentration on a fixed valid prime at every length, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A result conditional on a number-theoretic or complexity assumption must identify that assumption. Infinitely-often correctness, nonuniform advice, or ordinary randomized prime generation does not settle the stated unconditional question.
